transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-05-07
Start time (UTC): 16:00
Duration: ~48 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Nova VP Product), Ibrahim Khan (Nova ML Engineer), Ellen Park (Nova CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
- Nova Retail exploring hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC/on-prem) for conversational assistants and search ranking.
- Main constraints: monthly budget cap, latency SLOs (~200ms P50 for short queries), and audit/compliance for user data.
- Primary levers discussed: batching, KV/prefix caching, model quantization, dedicated capacity, routing fallbacks.
- Next: Redwood to send pricing model + benchmark checklist; Nova to share traffic profile and security contacts.

Topics:
- Per-token pricing and how batch size affects unit cost
- KV/prefix caching impact for repeat queries and product catalog context
- Dedicated capacity pricing structure and burst options
- Security: KMS, audit logs, SOC2, VPC private control plane

Transcript body (timestamps approximate, ASR imperfect):
00:00 Avery: Hey everyone thanks for joining, this is Avery from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, with Diego our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
00:06 Maya: Good thanks. We're excited. Short on time but want to make sure we cover economics.
00:11 Diego: Hi all, quick agenda — gather constraints, discuss levers (batching/caching/quant), hosting options, then next steps. Feel free to interrupt.
00:20 Ibrahim: Quick note — we care about P50 and P95 for latency, but budget drives decisions. We're doing a pilot for 3 months.
00:27 Ellen: And compliance — anything touching PII needs to be either on-prem or in a VPC with customer-managed keys. SOC2 is table stakes.
00:34 Avery: Understood. We'll show where Redwood Hosted can meet most cases and when Dedicated/Private is needed.

01:02 Diego: First, can you give a rough traffic profile? QPS, average tokens per request, and peak seasonality?
01:08 Ibrahim: Baseline 10 QPS average, peak 60 QPS during promos. Average prompt length 120 tokens, completion avg 40 tokens — so roughly 160 tokens per call. But distribution heavy tail — some sessions hit 600 tokens.
01:18 Diego: That's helpful. For unit economics we model per-token billing with batching. With 10QPS and batching windows we can sometimes group requests to reduce per-token compute overhead.
01:30 Maya: Can you explain how batching actually lowers cost? I thought faster meant fewer tokens?
01:35 Diego: Sure. Think of GPU utilization — each inference call has fixed overhead: kernel launch, attention setup, KV cache cost. When we batch, we amortize the overhead across multiple requests. So per-token cost goes down. But batching increases latency due to wait window.
01:50 Ibrahim: What's the typical latency penalty? We need ~200ms P50 for short queries.
01:56 Diego: With micro-batching tuned we can keep P50 within 150-200ms for short requests; P95 may increase depending on batch depth. We can configure latency SLOs: small batch windows for low-latency routes, larger batch windows for background rerank or embedding flows.
02:12 Maya: So a hybrid approach — low-latency hosted route for user-facing, batch route for async tasks?
02:16 Avery: Exactly, you can route by policy. Redwood's routing can send traffic to a low-latency pool or to a cost-optimized pool that uses larger batches and quantized models.

03:10 Ibrahim: You mentioned KV cache — would that help with our catalog-based assistant? We have lots of repeated prefixes.
03:16 Diego: Yes, prefix/KV caching is big for product catalogs. If you have many repeated beginning tokens (catalog context, user profile), we can cache KV for cached prefixes which cuts compute per request dramatically. In practice we see 20-60% token cost reduction for high prefix reuse.
03:32 Maya: Is that automatic? Any developer work?
03:36 Diego: It's semi-automatic — the runtime detects repeated prefixes and caches. You can also explicitly pin parts of context to the cache via our SDK. There's some instrumentation to see cache hit rates in the Console.
03:46 Ibrahim: Any constraints around cache eviction or multi-tenant noise?
03:50 Diego: For Hosted, caching is per-customer namespace; eviction governed by LRU and configured sizes. For Dedicated or Private you get more control and isolation.

05:00 Ellen: Let's talk numbers — baseline per-token price on Hosted and how Dedicated alters that.
05:07 Avery: Hosted per-token baseline varies by model family. For a mid-sized open model (similar to Llama-2-13B) pricing might be $0.0008 per prompt token and $0.0009 per completion token in a standard hosted tier — these numbers are illustrative. With batching and cache you could drive effective cost per served token down 25-50% depending on workload.
05:30 Maya: How does Dedicated pricing work? Is it still per-token or flat reserved capacity?
05:34 Avery: Dedicated is based on reserved GPU pools (monthly commit) plus a lower per-token compute fee for overage. So predictable monthly capacity rather than pure per-token. We provide cost modeling: you estimate average QPS, token distribution, and we'll show dedicated vs hosted TCO over 6-12 months.
05:49 Ibrahim: Can we do mixed — some routed to Hosted for burst or test and core traffic on Dedicated?
05:54 Diego: Yes, policy-based routing supports that. You can set fallback rules — e.g., if Dedicated pool saturated, fallback to a lower-cost hosted variant or to a smaller model.
06:05 Maya: What's the process for pilot? We have a $30k/month budget cap for testing.
06:10 Avery: Good. For pilot we propose a 6-week pilot: benchmarking week, integration week, and 4-week production pilot with clear token caps. We'll provide a cost model to keep you under budget and suggest quantized model configs to fit.

07:00 Ibrahim: Quantization — how much do we lose in quality and how much do we save?
07:05 Diego: Typical int8 or 4-bit quant saves 30-60% on inference throughput costs depending on kernel support. Quality drop depends on model; for many retrieval-augmented tasks quality remains very close, generative open-ended tasks may see more regressions. We recommend small evals with your prompt set; Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles.
07:22 Ibrahim: Can Redwood run the evals or will we run them?
07:25 Diego: We can run them as part of the pilot — provide prompt sets and we run comparative runs on hosted, quantized, and dedicated setups.

08:10 Maya: For compliance — if we need customer-managed KMS, is that supported in Hosted?
08:14 Avery: Hosted supports envelope encryption; for strict requirements Private (VPC) or Dedicated with customer KMS integration are available. Private gives you a customer-managed control plane and optional on-prem package.
08:25 Ellen: SOC2 — do you have reports we can share?
08:28 Avery: Yes, we'll share SOC2 Type II and ISO artifacts after an NDA. Diego will attach the security folder.

09:40 Ibrahim: Any limits around model size for Dedicated? We might want to test some 70B variants later.
09:45 Diego: Dedicated supports large models; kernel support and GPU sizing matter. For 70B you'll likely want multi-GPU sharding and specific kernel optimizations; that's where Dedicated shines because we control the pool sizing. Hosted can support large models but burst patterns and queueing differ.
09:59 Maya: Is there a price break for long-term Dedicated commits?
10:02 Avery: Yes, reserved capacity discounts for 6-12 month commitments, and enterprise pricing for annual. We usually model the break-even point given your token volume and latency needs.

11:30 Ibrahim: Let's run a simple hypothetical: 160 tokens per request average, 10QPS baseline. How much monthly token volume is that?
11:36 Diego: Rough calc: 10 QPS * 3600 * 24 * 30 = 25,920,000 requests/month. Times 160 tokens ≈ 4.15B tokens/month.
11:49 Ava... Avery: If that's accurate, Hosted costs at indexes we quoted would look like: 4.15B * $0.00085 ~= $3.5M/month — but that's raw and before batching/cache/quant savings. So you can see why batch/cache make or break feasibility.
12:06 Maya: Wait $3.5M is way over budget — our cap is $30k/month for pilot; our production expectation is much lower QPS or more aggressive caching.
12:13 Diego: Right, you likely won't sustain 10QPS of full 160-token work across entire user base; many queries will be short, and caching reduces effective tokens. Also routing to smaller models for simple queries helps.
12:24 Ibrahim: We need a more realistic traffic snapshot — we'll send exact telemetry.

13:40 Avery: We'll build a model with three scenarios: conservative (high cache hits + batching), moderate, and worst-case. We'll include Hosted, Dedicated, and Private TCOs. Does that work?
13:48 Maya: Yes. Also include a variant with heavy quantization and one with more routing to cheaper models.

14:20 Diego: One detail — if you want predictable latency, Dedicated with pinned pools reduces jitter from noisy neighbors. For low-latency user-facing routes we recommend small-batch pools pinned to a latency SLO.
14:32 Ibrahim: How do auto-scaling and burst credits work for Dedicated?
14:36 Avery: Dedicated has configurable autoscaling with reserved base capacity and burst buckets. You can set policies for scale-up thresholds. There's also burst allocation if you pay for additional burst capacity; we'll show cost tradeoffs for steady vs spiky traffic.

16:00 Maya: Any gotchas around embeddings and rerank costs? We have an embedding-heavy pipeline for search.
16:06 Diego: Embeddings are charged per input token (and/or per vector). You can batch embedding requests heavily — it's typically cheaper per item than generative tokens. Caching embedding vectors for repeated content also reduces compute. For rerank we recommend offloading expensive steps to larger batch windows.

18:10 Ibrahim: We want to run a 1-week benchmark: send 5k varied prompts and measure latency/cost across Hosted standard, Hosted quantized, and Dedicated. Possible?
18:16 Diego: Absolutely. We'll provide a benchmark harness and a checklist. We'll need sample prompts, expected prompts distribution, and target latency SLOs. We'll run on our infra and share raw traces.
18:25 Maya: Do you share token-level cost breakdown (model layer, GPU time, infra)?
18:29 Diego: Yes, Console shows token-level cost, latency breakdown, and model vs infra cost. We can export CSV for deeper analysis.

20:00 Ellen: On security docs — NDA first? How do we get SOC2 materials?
20:04 Avery: We'll send NDA if needed, but many customers accept a redacted SOC2 summary first. Diego will drop the security folder with artifacts and contact for our compliance team.

21:50 Ibrahim: A practical question — if we do Hosted pilot and later move to Dedicated, how hard is migration?
21:56 Diego: We aim for a consistent API/SDK so code changes are minimal. Model pinning and rollout policies transfer; the main work is in infra routing, CIDR/VPC configs, and any KMS or network egress rules. We can support a staged migration plan.
22:14 Maya: What about data residency — EU customers? We're US-based but have EU customers.
22:18 Avery: Private deployments or region-specific Dedicated deployments can satisfy residency. Hosted also offers region options in most cloud regions.

24:00 Ibrahim: Any mentionable limitations on audit logging or retention?
24:05 Diego: We support granular audit logs and configurable retention in Redwood Console for Dedicated and Private; Hosted default retention is 30 days, with add-on long-term retention as a paid option.

26:30 Maya: Who signs the PO and how fast can we get pilot access?
26:34 Avery: For small pilots we typically do an MSA + pilot addendum; standard procurement timeline is 2-4 weeks depending on legal. If needed we can do an evaluation agreement to move faster.

28:00 Ibrahim: Competitors — we've been talking to OpenAI and Anthropic for managed APIs, and Lambda Labs for self-host. Why pick Redwood?
28:09 Avery: Redwood sells as a production inference platform — the differentiator is control over unit economics (batching, cache, quant) + unified infra across hosted/dedicated/private. We also offer detailed observability and rollout tooling.
28:23 Maya: Any customers in retail we can reference?
28:26 Avery: We can share anonymized references; Diego will include a short case study about catalog assistant where caching saved ~40% cost.

30:10 Diego: Quick clarifying Q on your latency SLO: is 200ms P50 a hard requirement for core browsing flows, or scorable?
30:16 Maya: Hard for browsing UI; for search/async ranking we're ok with higher.
30:21 Diego: Great — that lets us carve routes.

31:45 Avery: Recap and commitments: we'll send pilot pricing and TCO model, Diego will share benchmark harness and security docs, Nova provides traffic profile and prompt set. We'll tentatively schedule the benchmark run week of 2026-05-18.
31:58 Maya: Sounds good. Also we'll confirm procurement timeline with our legal.

33:20 Ibrahim: Small nit — do you support SAML SSO and SCIM for provisioning?
33:24 Diego: Yes SSO (SAML/OIDC) and SCIM are supported for user provisioning in Console.

34:50 Ellen: On KMS: if we do customer KMS, are keys stored in our cloud KMS or do you support HSM?
34:55 Avery: We integrate with major cloud KMS providers and HSM-backed key stores for Private deployments. We'll outline options.

36:40 Maya: Anything else from Redwood side?
36:42 Diego: We'll include a sample config for batch windows, cache sizes, and a starter rollout policy. Also notes on model variants and fallback ordering.
36:52 Avery: I'll send pricing and a short pilot statement of work.

38:00 Maya: Ok thank you, this was helpful. One more question — if our pilot hits the $30k cap early, do you throttle?
38:06 Avery: We'll set hard token caps for pilot billing and alerts. We can also configure per-route caps so critical flows keep going while others throttle.

39:20 Ibrahim: We'll share the sample prompts and telemetry by Monday.
39:25 Maya: I'll loop in procurement. Ellen will follow up with security contacts.

40:00 Avery: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the items discussed.
